paper_title: Apriel Voice 27B Preview: An Open Model for Speech, Reasoning, and Tool Use

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A capable voice assistant must do more than recognize words; it must understand requests, reason over context, sustain conversations, and act through tools. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, an open speech-language model that unifies these capabilities within a shared reasoning backbone while retaining text and image input modalities. Built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, Apriel Voice directly processes speech and generates both responses and tool calls without requiring a separate dialogue model. We introduce a two-stage training procedure to adapt the model to speech. The first stage establishes the speech interface, while the second jointly adapts the projector and backbone through supervised fine-tuning, text replay, and source-dependent cross-entropy and forward Kullback--Leibler divergence supervision. Automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues provide conversational training data, while local teacher serving, overlapping teacher and student computation, and fused full-vocabulary losses enable efficient online distillation. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves a score of 98.90 on Big Bench Audio, 81.13 on Speech-BFCL, and a task success rate of 65.51% on $τ$-Voice, with a mean latency of 1.91 seconds. It also achieves 51.27% English EVA accuracy and 74.13% experience pass@1. Finally, we deploy Apriel Voice 27B Preview on a custom serving platform to support interactive voice interactions.

sections.title:
1
An employee reporting a locked account may describe the problem aloud, share a screenshot, correct an identifier,
and ask an assistant to open a ticket. The useful outcome is a resolved request: the assistant must connect
the evidence, follow the conversation, choose an appropriate action, and interpret the result. Supporting such
interactions requires speech understanding alongside the reasoning and tool use of a large language model (LLM).
sections.content: Recognition accuracy is necessary but insufficient for voice agent success. model may transcribe request correctly yet lack the ability to follow constraints or invoke the necessary tools to complete the associated task. Likewise, strong text performance does not establish that the same model can reason reliably when the request arrives as audio. We therefore evaluate speech as an interface to general capability, covering reasoning, instruction following, conversation, and task completion alongside recognition and translation [23, 4, 39]. Voice systems connect these capabilities in several ways. conventional 3-stage cascade combines automatic speech recognition (ASR), an LLM, and text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis, passing transcript to the reasoner. Speech-conditioned models instead expose the reasoner to learned acoustic features [28, 45, 43, 11]; native speech-generating models also integrate the output audio pathway [8, 51]. Another deployment pattern separates the spoken conversation from backend model responsible for reasoning and tools [34]. These designs allocate speech understanding, reasoning, synthesis, and interaction control to different components. We present Apriel Voice 27B Preview, or Apriel Voice in short, an open speech-language model built on the post-trained Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint [14, 15]. Apriel Voice uses the same reasoning backbone to understand speech, respond in conversation, and decide when and how to call tools. Text, images, and returned tool results remain part of its context (Figure 1). Speech synthesis is independently replaceable, allowing voices and deployment choices to change without retraining the reasoner. We release Apriel Live, an interactive interface enabling practitioners to experience Apriel Voice in real conversations. The training problem is to extend an already capable decoder with speech interface while preserving the behavior that makes it useful. We address it in two stages. Multilingual transcription, translation, and continuation first train speech projector with the backbone frozen. Broad supervised fine-tuning (SFT) then updates the projector and backbone using speech tasks, internally generated conversations, tool interactions, and text replay. Source-dependent cross-entropy (CE) and forward KullbackLeibler divergence (FKL) combine task targets with online supervision from frozen copy of the original backbone. The teacher supports learning during adaptation and is absent at inference. Contributions. This report brings together four contributions: 1. Broad speech-conditioned agentic capability. shared model handles spoken reasoning, instruction following, conversation, and tool-call generation while retaining text and image processing capabilities. 2. staged adaptation recipe. Speech interface learning with automatically constructed speech-conditioned dialogues and source-dependent CE/FKL supervision connects task acquisition with capability retention. 3. An efficient online-supervision implementation. Local teacher serving, overlap with student computation, fused full-vocabulary losses, and coordinated checkpointing support the combined training workload. 4. Evaluation and interactive deployment. Detailed results span speech, text, images, multilingual translation, service interactions, and enterprise workflows; Apriel Live demonstrates the corresponding application interface. In thinking mode, Apriel Voice achieves 98.90 on Big Bench Audio (BBA), 81.13 on BFCL, and 65.51% mean task success on τ -Voice. English EVA accuracy and experience pass@1 reach 51.27% and 74.13%. Together, these results show strong open-source (OSS) model whose speech capability extends to reasoning and action. The broader evaluation examines language coverage, reasoning-mode effects, and text and image retention. Table 5 summarizes the speech benchmarks; the following sections describe the method and detailed results.

2 Related Work
2.1 Connecting audio perception to language reasoning
Speech encoders provide transferable representations for recognition and downstream tasks [38]. SLAM-ASR
studies a simple learned connection between a speech encoder and a language model [28]; Ultravox develops a
speech-conditioned architecture with frame stacking and a learned projector [11]. SALMONN broadens the input
scope to speech, audio events, and music [43]. Apriel Voice 27B Preview follows this established encoder–projector
sections.content: 2 approach. Its emphasis is the capability of the adapted model across reasoning, instruction following, and complete interactions, evaluated together with recognition.

sections.title:
2.2 Transferring behavior across modalities
BLSP trains a speech adapter using continuations generated from text prefixes, and BLSP-KD transfers next-token
distributions between text and speech with token alignment and partial parameter adaptation [45, 46]. These
methods are direct precedents for teaching a language model to respond to speech through behavioral supervision.
Apriel Voice builds on that principle with staged interface learning, broad second-stage SFT, selected speech
distillation, and replay for a post-trained multimodal backbone. Supervision aligns the teacher’s and student’s
response positions; it does not require acoustic frames to match transcript tokens one to one.
sections.content: Our objective combines established forms of supervision: sequence targets [21], predictive-distribution distillation [19], and preservation of earlier behavior during adaptation [25]. The contribution lies in how these signals are selected and implemented across the speech and retention mixture. Similarly, synthetic instruction generation has precedent in Self-Instruct [48]. Our data pipeline converts internally generated task dialogues into speech-conditioned examples through automatic span selection, consistent reference voice within each conversation, and conversion-fidelity checks.

sections.title:
2.3 Speech generation and delegated voice systems
LLaMA-Omni combines speech perception, an instruction-tuned language model, and a streaming speech
decoder [10]. Moshi models concurrent user and assistant audio for full-duplex interaction [8], while Qwen3-Omni
integrates multimodal perception and speech generation in its Thinker–Talker design [51]. These output-generation
architectures differ from application-level delegation, in which a conversational voice model hands reasoning or
tool work to a separate backend [34].
sections.content: Apriel Voice places conversation, reasoning, and tool-call decisions in the same speech-conditioned backbone. Application components execute tools, return results to the same backbone, and synthesize response text. Turn detection and interruption control operate around the model.

sections.title:
2.4 Evaluating and training capable voice agents
EVA-Bench (EVA) measures both service accuracy and interaction experience [4], and τ -Voice evaluates task
completion under realistic audio conditions [39, 42]. τ 2-Bench and EnterpriseOps-Gym extend the evaluation to
text-agent interaction and stateful enterprise workflows [3, 29]. These benchmarks complement isolated recognition
and reasoning tests by asking whether an agent reaches the required outcome.
sections.content: For training, Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) distributes model state across workers [53], and fused-kernel systems such as Liger reduce the overhead of language-model operations [20]. Apriel Voice combines student sharding with local online-teacher execution, lookahead schedule, and full-vocabulary CE/FKL kernels. We describe these mechanisms together with the scale and duration of the completed training run.

3 Model Architecture
3.1 A shared backbone for perception, reasoning, and action
Apriel Voice 27B Preview starts from the instruction-tuned Gemma 4 26B-A4B checkpoint, a mixture-of-experts
model with approximately 26 billion total parameters and approximately four billion active parameters per
token [14, 15]. This backbone accepts text and images. We add a continuous speech interface while retaining its
output vocabulary, so spoken requests can elicit the same forms of response, reasoning, and tool calls as text
requests.
sections.content: Audio features, text tokens, image representations, and tool results condition the same backbone. The model generates either response to the user or tool call. The application executes tools, returns their results to the conversation, and sends response text to separate speech synthesizer.

3.3 Adapting the decoder while preserving its interfaces
Stage one trains the speech projector with the encoder and backbone fixed. Stage two updates the projector,
language backbone, and mixture-of-experts router together (Tab. 1). A frozen copy of the starting checkpoint
supplies online teacher distributions during training and is removed from the inference graph.

On text-only batches, zero-valued dependency keeps the projector in the distributed computation graph without adding speech information. The original vision tower and bridge remain frozen in both stages. Their outputs nevertheless pass through decoder that changes during stage two, so visual retention must be measured empirically. The text and image evaluations in Sec. 9 measure performance after adaptation.

4 Training Recipe
4.1 Two stages with complementary goals
Speech adaptation must solve two related problems: make acoustic input intelligible to an existing decoder, and
teach that decoder to use speech in complete tasks. We separate them in the training recipe (Figure 2). Stage one
learns the input interface through multilingual transcription, translation, and continuation. Stage two broadens
the task distribution and updates the backbone, with explicit supervision for acquiring new behavior and retaining
earlier capabilities.

7.1 Local teacher workers and sharded students
Teacher inference and student training have different resource requirements. The teacher performs forward
computation; the student also stores optimizer state and executes backward computation. We assign them
separate workers and use FSDP to shard student state [53].
Student workers send teacher contexts and position information to assigned teacher workers through GPU
point-to-point communication. The full-vocabulary path returns teacher logits in bfloat16 (BF16) format. This
traffic stays within a node, while student workers use distributed collectives across their own process group. The
same local allocation can therefore be repeated across nodes.
Stage-two training uses eight nodes, each with two teacher GPUs and six student GPUs: 16 teacher and 48
student NVIDIA H100 80 GB HBM3 GPUs overall. Training completed in approximately three days (Tab. 2).

7.2 Overlapping teacher and student computation
The training loop uses one-batch lookahead. After receiving the current teacher result, it issues the next request
before executing the current student computation. Teacher inference for batch k + 1 can then overlap student
forward and backward computation for batch k (Figure 4). The first teacher request primes the pipeline.

sections.title:
8 Evaluation Design
8.1 Questions and coverage
We structure our evaluation around three major research questions to establish whether a unified speech-language
backbone trained with our two-stage recipe can achieve competitive performance compared to leading open-source
and proprietary systems across reasoning, end-to-end task completion, and multimodal capability retention.
sections.content: RQ1: Whether Apriel Voice supports audio reasoning, instruction following, and tool use beyond foundational speech capabilities. One of the core contributions of speech-language models lies in their ability to process spoken instructions, reason over problems, and generate tool calls, not merely perform foundational speech recognition and translation. Therefore, we target evaluations across different foundational tasks (speech recognition, speech translation) and audio reasoning tasks, including instruction following (MT-Bench [54], IFEval [55]), reasoning over spoken questions (Big Bench Audio [18], Speech-GSM8K [7]), and tool-call capability via BFCL [37]. In addition, we continue to validate the foundational speech capabilities of the model: speech recognition (LibriSpeech [32], µ-Bench [24]) and speech translation (CoVoST 2 [44]). Accuracy and reasoning scores are reported on 0100 scale; WER can exceed 100%. RQ2: Whether those abilities translate into effective conversation and complete workflows. Beyond single-turn reasoning and instruction following, production systems must sustain multi-turn conversations, maintain context, and execute complete tasks through speech. To this end, EVA measures service accuracy and conversational experience, while τ -Voice evaluates task completion through speech [4, 39]. We complement these with τ 2-Bench for text-based agent interaction evaluation, and EnterpriseOps-Gym for testing stateful tool workflows [3, 29]. Together, these benchmarks distinguish between isolated correct answers and real-world complete task execution. RQ3: How text and image performance changes after adaptation. Text-input evaluations cover multidisciplinary knowledge and reasoning with MMLU-Pro [49], graduate-level science with GPQA Diamond [40], and mathematical problem solving with the American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME), MATH-500 [17], and the American Mathematics Competitions (AMC). Paired text/audio evaluations also test instruction following and tool use. Image evaluations cover optical character recognition (OCR), visual mathematics, multidisciplinary reasoning, charts, instruction following, and hallucination-related errors. Internal Gemma evaluations use the starting Gemma 4 26B-A4B backbone; published model-card results provide additional comparisons under their own evaluation settings.

10.2 Training and supervision
Interface training learns a projector that connects the frozen speech encoder to the fixed decoder. Task SFT
then adapts the projector and backbone for conversation and tool use. Source-dependent teacher supervision
supports adaptation on selected speech examples and retention on text replay. Paired text/audio dialogues provide
corresponding speech and text contexts for training.
sections.content: The systems implementation addresses the resulting cost: local teacher workers separate inference from student state, lookahead overlaps teacher and student computation, and fused losses reduce temporary probability storage. Together, these mechanisms support full-vocabulary online supervision at the training scale described in Tab. 2. The evaluations assess the combined method; component effects require controlled ablations.

sections.title:
11 Conclusion
Apriel Voice 27B Preview extends a text-and-image backbone to speech, using the same model for reasoning,
conversation, and tool-call decisions. Evaluations demonstrate these capabilities through spoken reasoning,
instruction following, multilingual translation, service interactions, and complete workflows.
sections.content: 18 The recipe combines interface learning, broad task SFT, synthetic speech-conditioned dialogues, and sourcedependent CE/FKL supervision. Local teacher serving, lookahead, and fused losses support online distillation. shared real-time API enables deployment and supports integration with voice benchmarks through WebSocket communication. Limitations Multilinguality. Apriel Voice 27B Preview prioritizes English speech understanding, reasoning, and instruction following for real-world English conversational-agent settings. Multilingual capabilities and evaluations remain limited, with primary assessment through automatic speech translation. English performance does not imply comparable quality across languages; multilingual robustness is uneven and can represent clear limitation. Enhancing multilingual speech understanding and conversational robustness across diverse language families is priority for future versions. Evaluation and comparison. Internal and public results differ in prompting, language coverage, output modality, reasoning budgets, judging, and task limits. Aggregate scores do not establish paired significance, non-inferiority to the starting backbone, or controlled ranking against every frontier system. Recognition means describe the evaluated language subsets; public and internal scoring can differ even when the language selection is shared. Data and attribution. Synthetic generation and distillation can propagate incorrect targets or teacher predictions. Conversion-fidelity checks can miss errors and do not establish coverage of natural speech variation. The evaluations characterize the combined recipe, with no causal attribution to individual data or supervision choices. Frozen visual components also do not guarantee unchanged image reasoning through an updated decoder. Transfer to other backbone families remains untested.

Each converted dialogue retains corresponding text version (Figure 3). Selection strategies. Whole-turn selection synthesizes the complete user message. Instruction-only selection does the same for generative requests without reference material. Question-only selection leaves reference material in text and speaks the question. Content-focused selection speaks material requested for reading or recitation. Multi-span selection speaks several disjoint intervals while retaining intervening text. configurable override adds whole-turn examples. Extraction validates selected source substrings before constructing the interleaved representation. Malformed selections are retried and rejected if the retry budget is exhausted. Voice assignment and chunking. reference utterance is assigned once per conversation and reused across its turns and chunks. Spoken-form conversion expands written expressions into pronounceable text. Sentence-based chunking respects duration limit. Contiguous chunks may be joined; disjoint spans retain their position among text. Speaker-aware scheduling and resumable processing preserve the reference assignment during generation. Conversion fidelity. Spoken-form judging compares normalized content with its source. Recognition-based judging compares synthesized chunks transcript with the intended speech. Optional turn-level faithfulness checks assess consistency across the complete converted turn.
